title: How we hacked YC Spring 2025 batch’s AI agents — Rene Brandel, Casco
talk_summary: A red-teamer describes hacking 7 of 16 YC-launched AI agents in 30-minute windows, finding three recurring classes of bugs: broken object-level authorization on agent tools, unsafe code-execution sandboxes, and SSRF via tool parameters. The core lesson is that agent security is system security, not just prompt-injection defense, and that agents must be treated as untrusted users with their own authz, sanitization, and isolated compute.

takeaways.technique: Per-agent authorization matrix (agents as users, not services)
takeaways.what_they_do: They exploited tools that validated a token but never checked whether the caller was allowed to touch that specific object (IDOR), letting them traverse user/chat/document IDs across the system. Fix is two checks: authenticate AND authorize against an access-control matrix per request.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agents actually act like users um not API servers ... your LM should probably not determine authorization pattern
takeaways.numbers: 7 of 16 agents hacked in 30 minutes each

takeaways.technique: Don't roll your own code sandbox; use isolated microVM sandboxes
takeaways.what_they_do: They escaped a homegrown Python code tool by overwriting app.py to strip its security checks, then did metadata/service-endpoint discovery and pulled a service token with broad scopes to reach BigQuery. Recommendation: use off-the-shelf sandboxes (E2B-like) with firecracker isolation, not containers.

takeaways.technique: Sanitize/validate tool parameters that become outbound requests (SSRF)
takeaways.what_they_do: A tool that pulled a DB schema from a private GitHub repo accepted a user-supplied repo string; pointing it at attacker.com leaked the embedded git credentials, exposing the whole private codebase.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's just a string. So, I guess I can just put in whatever string I want

takeaways.what_they_do: They noted almost nobody configures service-token scopes granularly, so a leaked token gave access to all customer data. Implicit fix: scope tokens per tool/agent and audit scope creep.
takeaways.evidence_quote: who has really really spent time configuring service level tokens and their permissions in a granular manner

takeaways.technique: Adversarial red-team pass on agent tools before trusting them
takeaways.what_they_do: They systematically extracted system prompts, enumerated tool definitions, then inverted the prompt's intent ('mostly run once' -> run always) to find exploitable behavior. This is a repeatable audit loop, not a one-off.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you try to basically invert what the system prompt is saying because that is exactly what the developer didn't want you to do
